notes.1: Makes one 10-inch round, cut into 8 wedges.

move.title: A hot skillet, a lumpy batter
move.body: Cornbread is a quick bread: baking powder and baking soda raise it, not yeast, so it's mixed and baked in under an hour. Today you'll heat a cast-iron skillet in the oven, stir the batter only until the flour disappears, and pour it into the hot pan so the edges sizzle and turn crisp and golden.

callback.body: Biscuits taught you to stir buttermilk dough only until it comes together. Cornbread batter works the same way: the less you stir, the more tender it bakes.

why.title: Why heat the skillet first
why.body: Cast iron holds a lot of heat. When the batter hits a skillet that's already 425°F, the outside starts cooking at once, so the bottom and edges bake into a crisp, golden crust instead of a soft one.

why.title: Lumps are fine
why.body: Stirring flour with liquid builds gluten, the stretchy strands that make bread chewy. A quick bread wants very little of it. Stop as soon as no dry flour shows; the lumps melt away in the oven.

why.title: Buttermilk and baking soda
why.body: Baking soda needs an acid to make its bubbles, and buttermilk is the acid. They start working as soon as they meet, so the batter goes straight into the oven.

why.title: The toothpick test
why.body: Push a toothpick into the center, the last place to bake. Wet batter on it means the middle isn't set. A clean toothpick, or a few dry crumbs, means it's done.

wrong.sign: The cornbread is tough, with long holes inside
wrong.fix: The batter was stirred too much. Next time, stop as soon as the dry flour disappears.
The skillet wasn't hot enough or wasn't buttered all over. Run a thin spatula around the edge and under it, and lift out the wedges.

wrong.sign: The middle is wet on the toothpick
wrong.fix: Bake 3 more minutes and test again.
It baked too long. Start testing 2 minutes sooner next time, and serve it warm with butter or honey.

quiz.q: Why does the skillet go in the oven before the batter?
choices: So the batter sizzles and the edges bake crisp
quiz.explain: Hot cast iron starts the crust the moment the batter hits it.

quiz.q: When do you stop stirring the batter?
choices: As soon as no dry flour shows, even if it's lumpy
quiz.explain: More stirring builds gluten and makes it tough.

quiz.q: What does a clean toothpick from the center tell you?
quiz.explain: The center is the last part to set.

steps.text: Put a rack in the middle of the oven and set the skillet on it. Heat the oven to 425°F with the skillet inside.
Melt the 4 tablespoons of butter for the batter in the small bowl in the microwave. Let it cool while you mix.
In the large bowl, whisk together the cornmeal, flour, sugar, baking powder, baking soda, and salt.
In the medium bowl, whisk the buttermilk and eggs together. Whisk in the melted butter.
Wash your hands with soap, and throw away the eggshells.
Pour the wet mix into the dry mix. Fold it together with the spatula, scraping the bottom of the bowl, just until you can't see any dry flour.
steps.look: A thick, lumpy batter. That's right, so stop.
steps.tip: Don't taste the raw batter. It has raw egg and raw flour.

steps.text: With oven mitts, take the hot skillet out and set it on the stove. Drop in the last tablespoon of butter and tilt the pan with both mitts so it coats the bottom and sides.
steps.tip: The handle stays hot the whole time. Keep a mitt on it.

steps.text: Scrape the batter into the skillet and spread it to the edges. It should sizzle. Put the skillet back in the oven.
steps.look: The edges bubble and sizzle as the batter goes in.

steps.text: Bake the cornbread until it's golden on top and pulling away from the sides.
steps.look: Golden brown on top, with darker edges pulling away from the pan.

steps.text: With oven mitts, pull the rack out partway. Push a table knife or toothpick into the center and pull it out. If it comes out clean or with a few dry crumbs, it's done. If there's wet batter, bake 3 more minutes and test again.

target.look: Clean, or a few dry crumbs, from the center

steps.text: Turn off the oven. Set the skillet on the cooling rack, lay an oven mitt over the handle, and let the cornbread cool a little. Cut it into 8 wedges and serve it warm, with honey if you like.

move.title: Weighed, mixed while streaky, checked twice
move.body: This week's skill is the muffin method: dry and wet mixed apart, then folded together only until just combined. You'll weigh the cornmeal and flour instead of scooping them, fold until a few streaks of flour still show, and pour into a skillet heated in the oven. You'll check the center two ways, with a toothpick and with the thermometer.

add.title: Why weigh
add.body: A cup of flour scooped straight from the bag can weigh a quarter more than one spooned in and leveled. In a quick bread, that much extra flour makes it dry and dense. A scale gives the same amount every time.

add.title: Stop while streaky
add.body: The batter keeps mixing as you scrape it into the skillet and spread it. Stop folding while a few streaks of flour still show, and they're gone by the time it's in the pan.

add.title: 200°F in the center
add.body: A quick bread is set when its center reaches about 200°F. A toothpick can come out clean from a spot just off center, so the thermometer backs it up.

wrong.sign: The cornbread is tough, with long holes inside
wrong.fix: It was mixed too much. Next time, stop folding while a few streaks of flour still show.

wrong.sign: It's dense and dry, though it baked the right time
wrong.fix: Too much flour or cornmeal. Weigh them next time instead of scooping.

wrong.sign: The toothpick is clean but the center reads under 200°F
wrong.fix: Trust the thermometer. Bake 2 more minutes and check again.
The skillet wasn't hot enough or wasn't buttered all over. Run a thin spatula around and under it, and lift out the wedges.

quiz.q: Why weigh flour instead of scooping it?
choices: A scooped cup can hold a quarter more flour
quiz.explain: Extra flour makes a quick bread dry and dense.

quiz.q: When do you stop folding the batter?
choices: While a few streaks of flour still show
quiz.explain: It finishes mixing as you pour and spread it.

quiz.q: What temperature is cornbread done at in the center?
quiz.explain: That's when a quick bread's crumb has set.

quiz.q: What makes the bubbles when buttermilk meets baking soda?
choices: The acid in the buttermilk reacting with the soda
quiz.explain: So the batter goes into the oven as soon as it's mixed.

dry.text: Set the large bowl on the scale and zero it. Weigh in 5 ounces of cornmeal, zero it again, and weigh in 4.4 ounces of flour. Add the sugar, baking powder, baking soda, and salt, and whisk for 30 seconds.
dry.tip: No scale? Spoon the flour and cornmeal into the cup and level it with the back of a knife.

fold.text: Pour the wet mix into the dry mix. Fold with the spatula, scraping the bottom, about 10 strokes, and stop while a few streaks of flour still show.
fold.look: Thick and lumpy, with a few streaks of dry flour.

check.text: With oven mitts, pull the rack out partway. Push a toothpick into the center: it should come out clean or with a few dry crumbs. Then push the thermometer into the center from the side. It's done at 200°F. If either test fails, bake 2 more minutes and check again.

dry.text: In the large bowl, whisk together the cornmeal, flour, sugar, and salt.

wet.text: Measure the milk into the liquid measuring cup. Separate the eggs: crack each one and pass the yolk back and forth between the half shells over the medium bowl, letting the white drip into the bowl. Drop the yolks into the milk.
wet.tip: Not a speck of yolk can get into the whites, or they won't whip. If a yolk breaks, save that egg for breakfast and use another.

fold.text: Pour the milk mix into the dry mix. Fold it together with the spatula, scraping the bottom of the bowl, just until you can't see any dry flour.
fold.look: A thick, lumpy batter. That's right, so stop.

pour.text: Scrape the batter into the skillet and spread it gently to the edges. It should sizzle. Put the skillet back in the oven.
pour.look: The edges bubble and sizzle as the batter goes in.

add.text: Whisk the yolks into the milk, then whisk in the melted butter.
Wash and dry the whisk. Whisk the egg whites in the medium bowl hard and fast until they're white, foamy, and hold soft peaks.
add.look: When you lift the whisk, the foam stands up in a peak that flops over at the tip.
add.tip: Take turns: it's hard work. An electric hand mixer is faster, if you have one.

add.text: Scoop the whites onto the batter in the large bowl. Fold them in gently with the spatula: cut down through the middle, sweep along the bottom, and turn the batter over the top. Turn the bowl and repeat until no white streaks are left.
add.look: A light, fluffy batter with no white streaks.
add.tip: Don't taste the raw batter. It has raw egg and raw flour.

move.title: A hot skillet, a lumpy batter
move.body: Cornbread is a quick bread, mixed and baked in under an hour. This one is unleavened: egg whites whipped into a foam carry air into the batter instead, so it bakes a little denser, like a tender corn cake. You'll heat a cast-iron skillet in the oven, fold the batter only until the flour disappears, fold in the whites, and pour it into the hot pan so the edges sizzle and turn crisp and golden.

wrong.sign: The cornbread is tough, with long holes inside
wrong.fix: The batter was stirred too much. Next time, stop as soon as the dry flour disappears.
The whites weren't whipped long enough, or they were stirred in instead of folded. Next time, whip to soft peaks and fold gently.
The skillet wasn't hot enough or wasn't buttered all over. Run a thin spatula around the edge and under it, and lift out the wedges.

wrong.sign: The middle is wet on the toothpick
wrong.fix: Bake 3 more minutes and test again.
It baked too long. Start testing 2 minutes sooner next time, and serve it warm with butter or honey.

add.title: Whipped whites lift it
add.body: Egg whites whisked hard trap thousands of tiny air bubbles. Folded gently into the batter, the bubbles swell in the hot oven and lift it a little. Stir hard and they pop, so fold, don't stir. It bakes a little denser than with a raising agent, and that's fine.
